persona.who: 25, Tamil-Singaporean analyst at a bank, first in family to go to university, got promoted early, feels she doesn't belong in the room.
persona.note: got promoted ahead of people with MBAs. in every meeting I think they're going to find out I'm just the girl from the HDB whose dad drove a taxi. I over prepare for everything and still feel sick before presenting

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call not feeling good enough, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: Seven days from proving you are not a fraud to standing in the truth that you are enough.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the replaying and the fear, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the verdict, not the MBA holders, is what keeps you sick before the room.
week_beats.steady: You hold that a promotion is not a loan, and that you are more than the story you tell yourself about where you came from.

understanding.core_struggle: Promoted ahead of others, she fears being exposed as a fraud and overprepares to hide it, yet still feels sick before presenting.
understanding.mirror: What you told us: got promoted ahead of people.
understanding.insight: You hold yourself to a standard you'd never put on someone you love, and you pay for it every day.

queries.hook: The weight of a fraud you cannot stop proving you are not, and the fear that one slip will expose the girl from the HDB. I feel like an imposter.
queries.diagnose: When a result goes wrong, the mind turns against itself; self-blame grows from believing the outcome alone measures our worth, and it turns honest effort into a performance.
queries.steady: A failure is something that happened, not who you are; no one who tries to do good is ever lost, and your worth is not their MBA.
queries.act: Lift yourself up instead of pushing yourself down; learn what this taught you, make amends where you can, and begin again.
queries.story: A woman of humble beginnings who rose to lead, faced the verdict of her own mind, and found the courage to stand in her own truth.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse.sanskrit: सहजं कर्म कौन्तेय सदोषमपि न त्यजेत् । सर्वारम्भा हि दोषेण धूमेनाग्निरिवावृताः ॥
verse.line: Don't abandon work that suits you just because it has flaws. Every undertaking has some, like fire has smoke.
verse.translation: One should not give up the work suited to one's nature, Kaunteya, even if it has faults; for all undertakings are clouded by faults, as fire is by smoke.
verse.why: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
verse.misuse: Not 'never change jobs'. It answers perfectionism, not a reason to stay where you're harmed.

prasang.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.
prasang.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna about finding peace in the work that is already yours. He tells him not to drop the duties that fit his nature just because they have imperfections. Every action has its flaws, Krishna says, just as every fire carries smoke. The point is to do what is yours, with its cracks and all, as an offering rather than a flawless performance.
verse.for_you: You got the promotion and you keep preparing until you are sick. That is the smoke around the fire of your own work. The work is yours. The fear is not proof that you do not belong there. Let the preparation be your offering and let the smoke clear on its own.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
verse.sanskrit: न त्वेवात्माऽवमन्तव्यः पुरुषेण कदाचन / न ह्यात्मपरिभूतस् भूतिर्भवति शोभना
verse.line: Never look down on yourself. Nothing good grows from self-contempt.
verse.translation: A person should never look down on himself. The one who despises himself never finds real prosperity.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

verse.meaning: Draupadi is telling Yudhishthira that waiting on fate is no plan. She says people must act. She tells him never to look down on himself. She says the one who despises himself never finds real prosperity. She means that you could do right for its own sake. Then you could work as if it all depends on you. The truth underneath is that your own judgment is what makes you sick.
verse.for_you: You are the one who decides if you are worthy. The verdict you keep rehearsing is what makes you sick before the room. You can step out from under that verdict today.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son Sanjaya, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: पुत्र नात्मावमन्तव्यः पूर्वाभिरसमृद्धिभिः / अभूत्वा हि भवन्त्यर्था भूत्वा नश्यन्ति चापरे / अमर्षेणैव चाप्यर्था नारब्धव्याः सुबालिशैः
verse.line: Don't look down on yourself because of past failures. Fortunes come and go, and can come again.
verse.translation: Son, don't look down on yourself because of past failures. Fortunes that never were come to be, and fortunes that were are lost. But don't start things out of mere resentment, like a fool.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Queen Vidula finds her son Sanjaya lying defeated after he has lost his kingdom. She tells him not to look down on himself because of past failures, because fortunes that never were can come to be, and fortunes that were can be lost. But she warns him not to start out of mere resentment, like a fool. The verse proposes that past failure does not define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.
verse.for_you: You hold that a promotion is not a loan, and that you are more than the story you tell yourself about where you came from. The comparison you keep with others is a habit, not a verdict. Let it be there without letting it write your next move.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: पातितोऽपि कराघातैरुत्पतत्येव कन्दुकः । प्रायेण साधुवृत्तनामस्थायिन्यो विपत्तयः ॥
verse.line: A ball knocked down bounces back up. For good people, setbacks rarely last.
verse.translation: A ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.
verse.misuse: Not a promise that suffering is always short, or that people who suffer long did something wrong.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari writes that a ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. He says the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last. He is not offering a magic cure. He is simply saying that the downward swing is not the whole story. The ball has a nature to rise again. The steady person does not stay on the ground.
verse.for_you: You are holding a promotion that feels like a borrowed thing. Let the ball fall. It will rise again, not because you are perfect, but because you are still moving on the path you are on.

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: पापं चेत्पुरुषः कृत्वा कल्याणमभिपद्यते / मुच्यते सर्वपापेभ्यो महाभ्रेणेव चन्द्रमाः
verse.line: Turn to doing good after a wrong, and you come out like the moon from behind a cloud.
verse.translation: If a person who has done wrong turns to doing good, he is freed from all his wrongs, like the moon coming out from behind a great cloud.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

prasang.title: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasang.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.meaning: Dharmavyadha, a meat-seller in Mithila, tells the ascetic Kaushika that if a person turns to doing good after a wrong, they are freed like the moon from behind a cloud. He is not talking about grand penance. He is talking about the ordinary work of caring for your parents and keeping envy away. The moon does not fight the cloud. It simply keeps its place until the cloud moves.
verse.for_you: This week, your work is to do one ordinary thing well. Care for the people in your life, and let your work speak for itself. The cloud will move.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥
verse.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.
verse.why: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.
verse.misuse: Not 'stay in the role your family or birth assigned you'. It's about being true to your own nature and calling.

prasang.title: The ignorant and the wise; act free of like and dislike
prasang.summary: Krishna contrasts the attached and the wise, warns that ego claims credit for what nature does, and says to follow your own path rather than imitate another's.
prasang.lesson: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna about action and the danger of borrowed lives. He says that doing your own duty, even if it is done imperfectly, is far better than perfectly performing someone else's duty. The path that belongs to you might have stumbles and rough edges, but it is yours. Walking a life that is not truly yours brings constant fear because the weight of it was never meant for you to carry.
verse.for_you: The overpreparing and the sick feeling before you present are signs of a borrowed life. You are trying to prove you belong in a role that was not truly yours to begin with, and that is what exhausts you.

story.title: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
story.story_hook: Everyone had named a number, and the one who could actually do it was sitting quietly at the back.
story.summary: At the ocean's edge, each monkey says how far he can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who has sat silent, and reminds him of his birth and power: why are you holding back? This is your time. Hanuman grows and prepares to leap.
story.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

anchor.speaker: Jambavan
anchor.setting: On the southern shore no one can leap the ocean; old Jambavan turns to the silent Hanuman.
anchor.sanskrit: बलं बुद्धिश्च तेजश्च सत्त्वं च हरिपुङ्गव। विशिष्टं सर्वभूतेषु किमात्मानं न सज्जसे।७।।
anchor.line: You have the strength, the brains and the courage. Why are you holding yourself back?
anchor.translation: Your strength, intelligence, energy and courage stand out among all beings, best of monkeys. Why do you not step up?
anchor.why: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

prasang.title: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
prasang.summary: At the ocean's edge, each monkey says how far he can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who has sat silent, and reminds him of his birth and power: why are you holding back? This is your time. Hanuman grows and prepares to leap.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone had named a number, and the one who could actually do it was sitting quietly at the back.
prasang.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

story.hook_title: Everyone said how far they could leap, and Hanuman sat silent at the back
story.teaser: Everyone said how far they could leap, and Hanuman sat silent at the back
story.for_you: Jambavan reminds Hanuman of the strength and courage he already has. You already hold the skill and the drive to do this work well. The part of you that feels like a fraud is simply a quiet voice that needs to be reminded that you are allowed to take up space.

script: You got the promotion and you keep preparing until you are sick. You see yourself as the girl from the HDB whose dad drove a taxi, and now you are terrified someone will find out you do not belong there. You are trying to outwork a fear that has already taken root inside you.

Arjuna is on the chariot, and Krishna is teaching him about the duties that belong to each person by their own nature. Krishna tells Arjuna that no work is perfect. Every action has its flaws, just as every fire has smoke. And Krishna replied:
सहजं कर्म कौन्तेय सदोषमपि न त्यजेत्, सर्वारम्भा हि दोषेण धूमेनाग्निरिवावृताः.
In plain words: Don't abandon work that suits you just because it has flaws. Every undertaking has some, like fire has smoke.

This is about letting the smoke be there. You believe that if you prepare enough, the smoke will vanish and you will prove you are not a fraud. But Krishna says every fire produces smoke. The smoke is not a sign that the fire is wrong. It is simply part of the work. You cannot remove the flaws from your work, and you cannot remove the fear from your mind. You can only keep doing the work that is already yours, with all its cracks, and let the smoke clear on its own time.
Tomorrow, when the presentation comes, let your preparation be enough. Do not try to erase the smoke. Do the work as an offering, and trust that the work itself is what brought you to this seat.
What if the smoke was never a sign to run.

depth.life: You got the promotion ahead of others. You see yourself as the girl from the HDB whose dad drove a taxi. You overprepare for everything and still feel sick before presenting, as if the work is a costume you are waiting to be found out in.
depth.points: Krishna tells Arjuna that every undertaking is clouded by faults, like fire by smoke. The flaw is not a sign to abandon the work. It is the natural shadow of any action. Your anxiety is the smoke of your own capable fire. The work fits you. The flaw does not disqualify you.
depth.practice: Before your next presentation, name one flaw in your preparation and set it aside. Do not fix it. Let it be smoke.
depth.question: What would happen if you did the work and let the smoke rise?
